s: The fragments preserve broken passages from lost books of Diodorus Siculus. They include material on theology, Panch(a)ia, Corinthian rulers, and the origins of Rome.

l: Evemerus the Messenian, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, TH£BMBi«
s: Evemerus the Messenian is described as a friend of King Cassander who undertook long voyages and reached islands in the ocean, including Panch(a)ia. He wrote a sacred history arguing that some gods were immortal while others were earthly humans honored for their benefits to mankind.

l: Panch(a)ia, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, TH£BMBi«
s: Panch(a)ia is described as the largest of certain islands in the ocean reached by Evemerus. Its inhabitants were devoted to religion, and the island contained a temple of Jupiter Triphylius with a golden pillar recording the deeds of Uranus, Saturn, and Jupiter.

l: Uranus, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, TH£BMBi«
s: Uranus is presented in Evemerus’s account as the first king, a just and good man skilled in astrology. He was said to have first worshipped the heavenly gods and to have fathered Pan, Saturn, Rhea, and Ceres with Vesta.

l: Corinthian kingdom, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, TH£BMBi«
s: The Corinthian kingdom was founded after the Dorians’ return, when the Heraclids gave Corinth and its neighboring territory to Alethes. A succession of rulers followed him until Cypselus ended the established form of government.

l: Corinth, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, TH£BMBi«
s: Corinth was enlarged by Alethes, who reigned there for thirty-eight years. After the royal succession ended, the Bacchidae governed together with equal authority and annually appointed one of themselves as Prytanis until Cypselus.

l: Romans, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, TH£BMBi«
s: The Romans are discussed in a fragment concerning their origins. The account rejects the claim that Romulus was the son of Aeneas and places the building of Rome many generations after Aeneas.

l: Romulus, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, TH£BMBi«
s: Romulus is identified as the builder of Rome. The fragment states that he could not have been the son of Aeneas because many kings reigned between Aeneas and Romulus.

l: Rome, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, TH£BMBi«
s: Rome is said to have been built in the second year of the seventh Olympiad, more than 430 years after the Trojan War. The fragment contrasts this chronology with the erroneous claim that Romulus was the son of Aeneas.

l: Aeneas, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, TH£BMBi«
s: Aeneas gained the kingdom of the Latins three years after Troy was destroyed and reigned for three years before being worshipped as a god. He was also said to have been guided toward the site of a future city by a white sow, though the account identifies this tradition as coming from Fabius.

l: sacred history, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, TH£BMBi«
s: Sacred history is the work attributed to Evemerus in which he wrote specifically about terrestrial deities. The unit summarizes its account of gods such as Hercules, Dionysius or Bacchus, Aristaeus, Uranus, Saturn, and Jupiter.

l: The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, BOOK XXI,
s: The unit warns especially against covetousness and recounts how ambition, fraud, revenge, and cruelty brought disasters to rulers and cities. Antigonus, king of Asia, was defeated and killed after making war against Ptolemy Lagus, Seleucus, Lysimachus, and Cassander, while Agathocles conquered Crotona through deception and conducted campaigns in Italy. Agathocles was later poisoned and killed through the plotting of Archagathus and Menon of Aegista, after which the Syracusans restored their democracy. Foreign soldiers then massacred their hosts and seized Messana, naming it Mamertina.

l: covetousness, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, BOOK XXI,
s: Covetousness is described as a vice especially to be avoided because hopes and desire of gain prompt injustice and cause great mischiefs. It can involve both mean men and kings in extreme calamities.

l: Demetrius, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, BOOK XXI,
s: Demetrius, the son of Antigonus, fled with Stratonice and their wealth to Cyprus after Antigonus was killed. He later killed Alexander, the brother of Antipater, and also killed Antipater, who had murdered his own mother. Demetrius received Agathocles's son kindly, gave him royal gifts, and sent Oxythemes with him as a spy.

l: Crotona, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, BOOK XXI,
s: Agathocles deceived Crotona by claiming that he was sending his daughter Lanassa to Epirus to marry. He besieged the city, breached it through mines and batteries, and after its gates were opened his soldiers plundered the houses and killed the men.

l: Syracuse, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, BOOK XXI,
s: Syracuse was the seat of Agathocles's power and later regained its democratic government after his death. The Syracusans confiscated his estate, destroyed his statues, and resisted Menon and the foreign soldiers.

l: Menon of Aegista, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, BOOK XXI,
s: Menon of Aegista was a captive servant and intimate of Agathocles who secretly hated him because of the destruction of his country and his own dishonourable treatment. At Archagathus's urging, Menon poisoned Agathocles with a tooth-picker. He later murdered Archagathus and tried to gain control by winning the army to his side.

l: Carthaginians, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, BOOK XXI,
s: The Carthaginians had gained control of the sea and secured their country from invasion. They later joined Menon against the Syracusans, forcing the Syracusans to make peace, provide four hundred hostages, and restore the exiles.

l: Messana, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, BOOK XXI,
s: Foreign soldiers expelled from Syracuse went to Messana, where they were received as friends and confederates. They massacred their hosts at night, married their wives, and seized the city.

l: Mamertines, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, BOOK XXI,
s: The foreign soldiers who seized Messana called the city Mamertina, taking the name from Mars, whom they called Mamers in their own country language.

l: war, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, BOOK XXI,
s: War is presented as uncertain because folly and fraud can sometimes accomplish as much as courage. The unit also describes wars involving Antigonus, Agathocles, Menon, the Carthaginians, and the Syracusans.

l: Antigonus's war against the four kings, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, BOOK XXI,
s: Antigonus's war against Ptolemy Lagus, Seleucus, Lysimachus, and Cassander ended with Antigonus's death in battle. Demetrius and Stratonice then fled with their wealth to Cyprus.

l: sack of Crotona, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, BOOK XXI,
s: The sack of Crotona followed Agathocles's deceptive siege. After the Crotoneans opened the gates out of fear, his soldiers plundered the houses and killed all the men.

l: Agathocles's Italian campaign, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, BOOK XXI,
s: Agathocles's Italian campaign included an expedition with thirty thousand foot soldiers and two thousand horse. He ordered attacks on the Brutii, lost ships in a storm, captured Hipponium, took hostages, and temporarily returned to Syracuse.

l: death of Agathocles, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, BOOK XXI,
s: Agathocles's death resulted from poison placed by Menon on a tooth-picker at Archagathus's direction. He suffered a spreading corruption of his gums and teeth, was unable to speak, and was burned alive by Oxythemes; the Syracusans then restored their democracy and confiscated his property.

l: Syracusan democracy, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, BOOK XXI,
s: The Syracusan democracy was restored after Agathocles's death. The Syracusans confiscated Agathocles's goods and estate and broke down his statues.

l: massacre and seizure of Messana, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, BOOK XXI,
s: The massacre and seizure of Messana was carried out by foreign soldiers who had been welcomed as friends and confederates. They killed their hosts during the night, married their wives, seized the city, and called it Mamertina.

l: The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, BOOK XXII.
s: The unit describes Pyrrhus's intervention in Sicily, where he reconciled the factions at Syracuse, gained control of Agrigentum and many other cities, and conquered most Carthaginian possessions except Lilybaeum. The Carthaginians resisted his siege of Lilybaeum, forcing him to withdraw and plan to build a fleet for an invasion of Africa. It also recounts the rise and fall of Sicilian rulers, including Hicetas, Phintias, Thynion, Sosistratus, and Hiero, as well as the defeat and destruction of Brennus and the Gauls. Hiero later defeated the Mamertines near Messana, but Hannibal intervened and secured Messana from immediate surrender.

l: Pyrrhus, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, BOOK XXII.
s: Pyrrhus was invited to Sicily by Thynion and Sosistratus and landed there while the Carthaginians besieged Syracuse. He reconciled Thynion, Sosistratus, and the Syracusans, received ships, weapons, soldiers, and support from many cities, and conquered most Carthaginian possessions in Sicily. He failed to take Lilybaeum after a two-month siege and then planned to build a fleet and transport an army into Africa.

l: Mamertines, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, BOOK XXII.
s: The Mamertines had treacherously murdered the inhabitants of Messana and later allied themselves with the Carthaginians against Pyrrhus. Hiero defeated their army near the river Lotanus, killing nearly all of them and capturing their general Cion. Hannibal then made a league with them and reinforced Messana with soldiers.

l: Messana, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, BOOK XXII.
s: Messana was held by the Mamertines, who were nearly forced to surrender after Hiero defeated their army. Hannibal prevented the surrender, made a league with the Mamertines, and reinforced the city.

l: Hicetas, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, BOOK XXII.
s: Hicetas ruled Syracuse for nine years and defeated Phintias at Hibleum. He later suffered defeat by the Carthaginians at the river Terias and was deprived of Syracuse by Thynion.

l: Syracuse, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, BOOK XXII.
s: Syracuse was besieged by the Carthaginians by land and sea and appealed to Pyrrhus for aid. Pyrrhus entered the city without opposition, reconciled its factions, and received its ships, engines, weapons, and provisions. Syracuse later supplied the siege engines and arms used in Pyrrhus's campaign against the Carthaginians.

l: Phintias, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, BOOK XXII.
s: Phintias, tyrant of Agrigentum, defeated Hicetas's forces before later suffering hostility from the cities under his rule. He built Phintia, settled the displaced Gelans there, and was represented in a dream as being killed by a boar.

l: Agrigentum, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, BOOK XXII.
s: Agrigentum was ruled by Phintias and later commanded by Sosistratus. Pyrrhus received Agrigentum and its forces from Sosistratus, gaining eight thousand foot soldiers and eight hundred horse, along with control of thirty cities.

l: Carthaginians, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, BOOK XXII.
s: The Carthaginians fought Hicetas, besieged Syracuse with a fleet and a large land army, and formed a league with the Romans. They resisted Pyrrhus at Lilybaeum with abundant troops, supplies, fortifications, and engines, preventing him from taking the city. They later joined Hiero in a confederacy to besiege Messana.

l: Gauls, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, BOOK XXII.
s: The Gauls under Brennus invaded Macedonia and Greece with a very large army and intended to plunder the temple at Delphi. After suffering heavy losses, they retreated, but Greek attacks, hunger, cold, and further fighting destroyed the army so completely that none returned home.

l: Brennus, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, BOOK XXII.
s: Brennus led the Gauls into Macedonia and Greece and suffered many losses and three serious wounds during the fighting. Near death, he advised the Gauls to kill the wounded, burn the carriages, return home, and make Cichorius king; he then killed himself after drinking wine.

l: Thynion, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, BOOK XXII.
s: Thynion, son of Mameus, deprived Hicetas of Syracuse after Hicetas had ruled there for nine years. He later controlled the island portion of Syracuse and joined Sosistratus in sending for Pyrrhus; Pyrrhus subsequently reconciled the two rulers.

l: Sosistratus, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, BOOK XXII.
s: Sosistratus ruled the Syracusans and controlled Agrigentum and many other cities. He and Thynion sent for Pyrrhus, and Sosistratus later surrendered Agrigentum and its soldiers to him. Pyrrhus reconciled Sosistratus with Thynion and the Syracusans.

l: Lilybaeum, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, BOOK XXII.
s: Lilybaeum was built by the Carthaginians after Dionysius ruined Motya. It was strongly fortified and supplied by sea, resisted Pyrrhus's assaults and undermining attempts, and remained in Carthaginian possession after he raised the siege.

l: Hiero, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, BOOK XXII.
s: Hiero captured Myle and Amesalus, destroyed Amesalus, and then took Alese while gaining the submission of Abaceni and Tyndaridae. He defeated the Mamertines near the river Lotanus, but Hannibal's intervention discouraged him from besieging Messana, so he returned to Syracuse. He later entered a confederacy with the Carthaginians to besiege Messana.

l: Hannibal, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, BOOK XXII.
s: Hannibal, the Carthaginian general, went to Hiero after the defeat of the Mamertines, apparently to congratulate him but actually to deceive him. He then went to Messana, persuaded the Mamertines not to surrender, made a league with them, and reinforced the city with soldiers.

l: Sicily, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, BOOK XXII.
s: Sicily contained several independent rulers and cities engaged in frequent wars and plundering. Pyrrhus gained control of much of the island, taking or receiving numerous cities and driving the Carthaginians from their possessions except Lilybaeum.

l: Pyrrhus's Sicilian campaign, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, BOOK XXII.
s: Pyrrhus's Sicilian campaign began when he sailed from Tarentum to aid Syracuse against the Carthaginians. He gained support from Taurominium, Catana, Syracuse, Agrigentum, and many other cities, conquered Heraclea, Azone, Egesta, Panormus, and other places, and reached the Carthaginian possessions near Lilybaeum. The campaign failed to capture Lilybaeum, after which Pyrrhus planned to obtain naval superiority and invade Africa.

l: Carthaginian siege of Syracuse, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, BOOK XXII.
s: The Carthaginians besieged Syracuse by land and sea with one hundred ships and fifty thousand men. They enclosed the city, ravaged the surrounding countryside, and forced the Syracusans to appeal to Pyrrhus for aid. Pyrrhus's arrival caused the Carthaginians to withdraw their ships and allowed him to enter Syracuse without opposition.

l: siege of Lilybaeum, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, BOOK XXII.
s: Pyrrhus besieged Lilybaeum after taking most of the other Carthaginian possessions in Sicily. The Carthaginians reinforced the city from Africa with troops, grain, engines, and weapons, and strengthened its landward defenses. After repeated assaults and attempts to undermine the walls failed, Pyrrhus raised the siege after two months.

l: The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, BOOK XXIIL
s: The unit describes the early struggle between the Romans, Carthaginians, and their allies for control of Sicily, beginning with the siege of Messana and the Roman intervention. Hiero made peace with Rome for fourteen years, while the Romans and Carthaginians continued campaigns against cities including Agrigentum, Mytistratus, Camarina, Enna, and Panormus. The Carthaginians later defeated a Roman army in Africa under Attilius after hiring Xanthippus, and Roman fleets suffered major shipwrecks near Camarina and elsewhere. The unit ends with Cecilius defeating Asdrubal's undisciplined Carthaginian army at Panormus and capturing sixty elephants.

l: Sicily, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, BOOK XXIIL
s: Sicily is described as one of the finest islands in the world and as strategically capable of supporting the growth of a larger dominion. It becomes the principal theater of the war between the Romans, Carthaginians, and their allies.

l: Hanno, the son of Hannibal, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, BOOK XXIIL
s: Hanno, the son of Hannibal, landed in Sicily, assembled his forces at Lilybaeum, marched to Selinus, fortified the citadel at Agrigentum, and brought its people into alliance with the Carthaginians. He later joined Hiero in besieging Messana, but the Roman intervention forced Hiero to withdraw to Syracuse.

l: Hiero, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, BOOK XXIIL
s: Hiero allied with the Carthaginians against the Romans and joined in the siege of Messana. He argued that the Mamertines deserved to be besieged because of their violence and seizure of Messana, but he later made a fourteen-year peace with Rome, retaining Syracuse and the cities under his jurisdiction. He also supplied Roman forces with siege engines and other instruments of war and courteously aided Roman survivors of the shipwreck near Camarina.

l: Carthaginians, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, BOOK XXIIL
s: The Carthaginians fought throughout Sicily against the Romans, besieged Messana, and held or recovered several Sicilian cities. They lost Agrigentum but later brought a large army from Africa under Hanno the elder, replaced Hanno with Amilcar after a defeat, and achieved a major victory over the Romans in Africa through Xanthippus. Their forces also captured Agrigentum after a Roman shipwreck and later suffered defeat at Panormus.

l: Romans, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, BOOK XXIIL
s: The Romans intervened at Messana, sent an army under Appius Claudius, and expanded their control over many Sicilian cities. They made peace with Hiero, captured or destroyed several towns, took Agrigentum, and repeatedly attacked Carthaginian positions. They suffered a major defeat in Africa under Xanthippus and severe naval losses in storms, including the shipwreck near Camarina, but later captured Panormus.

l: Agrigentum, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, BOOK XXIIL
s: Agrigentum was fortified by Hanno, the son of Hannibal, and its people were brought over to the Carthaginian interest. The Romans later besieged and captured it after a stout resistance, while a subsequent Carthaginian force under Carthalo again took and burned the town and demolished its walls.

l: Messana, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, BOOK XXIIL
s: Messana was besieged jointly by Hiero and the Carthaginians after the Roman intervention there. Appius Claudius arrived from Rhegium, and the Roman presence caused Hiero to withdraw to Syracuse.

l: Syracuse, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, BOOK XXIIL
s: Syracuse was threatened when the Romans marched against Hiero after receiving the submission of many cities. Hiero negotiated peace with the Roman consuls, and Syracuse remained in his hands along with the other cities under his jurisdiction.

l: Hanno the elder, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, BOOK XXIIL
s: Hanno the elder brought an army of fifty thousand infantry, six thousand cavalry, and sixty elephants from Africa into Sicily after the siege of Agrigentum. He marched from Lilybaeum to Heraclea, suffered losses in two battles, and lost thirty elephants, after which the Carthaginians fined him six thousand pieces of gold, removed him from command, and replaced him with Amilcar.

l: Amilcar, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, BOOK XXIIL
s: Amilcar was sent to Sicily as general in place of Hanno the elder. He defeated the Romans at Thermæ, captured or received several places through betrayal, strengthened Drepanum, and destroyed Eryx except for the part surrounding its temple.
